title: A single domestication for maize shown by multilocus microsatellite genotyping
authors: Matsuoka Y., Vigouroux Y., Goodman M.M., Sanchez G.J., Buckler E., Doebley J.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: all maize arose from a single domestication in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago
summary: Phylogeny of 264 plants genotyped at 99 microsatellites places all maize in one lineage derived from Balsas-drainage teosinte (ssp. parviglumis), against earlier multiple-origin proposals. Also infers spread from the Mexican highlands over the Americas along two paths.
limits: Genetic inference from modern landraces, not a dated archaeological sample; the 9,000-year figure is a model estimate. Does not address South American secondary improvement (see Kistler 2018).

strand.to: Americas (highland Mexico, then lowlands and South America)

title: Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize from the Central Balsas River Valley, Mexico
authors: Piperno D.R., Ranere A.J., Holst I., Iriarte J., Dickau R.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: indicate that maize was present by 8,700 calendrical years ago
summary: Starch grains and phytoliths from the Xihuatoxtla shelter (Guerrero) show maize in the Balsas valley, where its wild ancestor is native, by 8,700 cal BP, with early domesticated squash.
limits: Microfossil identification at a single shelter; shows presence and use, not the whole spread. Companion excavation paper is Ranere et al. 2009.

summary: Excavation report for the Xihuatoxtla shelter: stone tool assemblage radiocarbon dated to at least 8700 cal BP, with the maize and squash residues in contemporaneous or underlying contexts.

title: Multiproxy evidence highlights a complex evolutionary legacy of maize in South America
authors: Kistler L., Maezumi S.Y., Gregorio de Souza J., et al.
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: spread into South America by ~6500 yr B.P.
summary: Genomes of landrace and archaeological maize indicate a partially domesticated population left Mexico, crossed Central America (~7500 BP) and was improved in the southwestern Amazon; multiple human-mediated dispersals followed.
limits: Only the repository abstract was opened (Science page not opened, see notes). Complicates the single-trajectory picture of Matsuoka 2002; Piperno/Kistler-school dating of the Mexican start is shared.

title: Domestication and lowland adaptation of coastal preceramic maize from Paredones, Peru
authors: Vallebueno-Estrada M., Hernandez-Robles G.G., Gonzalez-Orozco E., et al.
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: ancient Peruvian maize originated in Mesoamerica as all landraces found to date, followed by a rapid dispersal into the lowlands of South America
summary: DNA from three Paredones cobs dated ~6700-5000 cal BP ties Peruvian maize to a Mesoamerican origin with local lowland adaptation.
limits: Three specimens from one site; dates and ancestry are as reported by the authors.

title: Mesoamerican Metallurgy: the Perspective from the West
venue: In Roberts B.W., Thornton C.P. (eds), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective, Springer
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: metallurgy was introduced from the south, along the Pacific coast, from Northern South America and also from Colombia and Lower Center America
summary: Hosler's own synthesis: West Mexican metalwork first appears c. 700 CE and Mesoamerica is 'an unambiguous case of technology transfer' from the south, shaped by local preference for sound and colour.
limits: Only the abstract was readable (chapter paywalled). Author is the proponent; no independent sceptical paper on the Ecuador-West Mexico maritime link was opened. Route and mechanism are inferred from technical comparison, not documented by a dated text.

title: Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: a single contact event occurred in eastern Polynesia, before the settlement of Rapa Nui
summary: Genome-wide data (807 individuals, 17 Polynesian islands) show Native American ancestry related to Colombian groups in eastern Polynesia, dated about 1150-1230 CE depending on island; the paper notes the sweet potato debate.
limits: Modern DNA; the Rapa Nui estimate (1380 CE) is later and may be inflated by later Chilean admixture; the paper itself notes critics who hold the sweet potato dispersal need not be human-mediated. Route and direction (Polynesians to America and back, or Americans to Polynesia) are not fixed.

strand.from: Native American group related to present-day Colombia

title: Did ancient Americans settle in Polynesia? The evidence doesn't stack up
ask_addressed: State what is documented, inferred and disputed for each, and quote the main sceptical papers.
quote: The suggestion that it was Native Americans who made the voyage, however, is where we think this argument goes off the rails.
summary: Specialists accept contact c. 1200 CE (and the sweet potato) but argue Polynesian voyagers, not Native Americans, made the journey, citing absent archaeology and demographic limits of modern-DNA dating.
limits: Expert commentary, not a peer-reviewed reanalysis; authors disclose Royal Society of New Zealand funding and are Polynesian-origins specialists with their own position.

title: Ancient and historic dispersals of sweet potato in Oceania
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (commentary)
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: Archaeological research has now conclusively shown that the sweet potato was introduced to Central Polynesia by approximately A.D. 1200 to 1300
summary: Commentary on Roullier et al. 2013: the American crop reached Central Polynesia by 1200-1300 CE, most likely carried by Polynesian voyagers who reached South America.
limits: Commentary, not the genetic study itself; the human-vector claim is contested (the 2020 Ioannidis paper notes critics of human-mediated dispersal). The Munoz-Rodriguez 2018 sceptical paper was not opened.

title: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021
authors: Kuitems M., Wallace B.L., Lindsay C., et al.
ask_addressed: Americas: maize domestication and spread, Andean-Mesoamerican metallurgy contact, Polynesian-Native American contact (Ioannidis 2020 aDNA and the sweet potato), Norse contact in Newfoundland (L'Anse aux Meadows 1021 CE dendro date, Kuitems 2022), the Columbian Exchange.
quote: Here we provide evidence that the Vikings were present in Newfoundland in AD 1021
summary: Radiocarbon ring series from Norse-cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows, matched to the 993 CE cosmic-ray spike, give a felling year of 1021 CE on three trees.
limits: Dates one site's wood only; the authors call it a chronological anchor. Does not itself show who the Norse met or whether they stayed.

title: Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021 (scope and genetic exchange)
authors: Kuitems M., Wallace B.L., Lindsay C., et al.
ask_addressed: State what is documented, inferred and disputed for each, and quote the main sceptical papers.
quote: Recent data from the Norse Greenlandic population, however, show no evidence of the last of these
summary: Same paper, a separate caution: sagas imply cultural exchange with Indigenous people, but Norse Greenlandic genomes show no sign of the exchange of human genetic information.
limits: Listed separately only for the sceptical point; one paper, sourced to its own ref. 8 (not opened). Absence of Native American ancestry in Greenland does not rule out contact elsewhere.
